questions.q: According to Mill, why isn't democracy by itself enough to protect personal freedom?
a: Because the majority can impose its views on individuals
Because elected officials ignore the law once in office
Because voters lack the education to choose wisely
Because constitutions concentrate power in one leader
questions.why: Lesson 1 argues that majority rule can still threaten the individual through what Mill calls social tyranny.

questions.q: What does Mill call the majority forcing its opinions and beliefs onto people who disagree?
a: Social tyranny
Legal tyranny
Economic coercion
Moral licensing
questions.why: Lesson 1 names social tyranny as the majority imposing its opinions, views and beliefs on dissenters.

questions.q: Which action would Mill say justifies limiting someone's freedom?
a: Pulling a person away from an oncoming train
Stopping someone from voicing an unpopular opinion
Requiring everyone to follow the majority religion
Forcing someone to adopt the majority's customs
questions.why: Lesson 2 says interference is justified to prevent harm, such as pulling someone away from a nearby train.

questions.q: Why does Mill argue that false opinions are valuable?
a: They force society to re-examine why its common beliefs are right
They make it easier for everyone to agree on the truth
They protect the majority from criticism
They keep people from changing their customs
questions.why: Lesson 3 explains that wrong opinions force society to re-examine whether its common beliefs are actually correct.

questions.q: What are the three scenarios in which Mill says interference can prevent harm?
a: Harm by default, omission and accident
Harm by speech, trade and religion
Harm by nature, poverty and disease
Harm by majority, minority and state
questions.why: Lesson 2 separates justified interference into harm that comes by default, by omission and by accident.
